questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic with a draining lesion on his forearm. Gram stain of the purulent drainage shows purple-staining spherical bacteria arranged in irregular, grape-like clusters. Which of the following genera do these organisms most likely belong to?

explanation.summary: Staphylococci are gram-positive cocci that characteristically clump in grape-like clusters.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococci stain purple because they are gram positive, they are spherical, and they tend to cluster together like grapes rather than forming pairs or chains. This appearance in pus is the first clue to the genus. Because all staphylococcal species look identical on Gram stain, biochemical testing is needed to identify the species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clostridium species are gram-positive, spore-forming rods rather than cocci in clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corynebacterium species are gram-positive bacilli and would appear as purple rods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neisseria species are gram negative, stain pink, and appear as diplococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococci are also gram-positive cocci, but they are arranged in chains rather than clusters.

questions.stem: A laboratory isolates gram-positive cocci from a wound culture and must determine whether the organisms belong to the genus Staphylococcus rather than Streptococcus or Enterococcus. Which of the following tests is most useful for this distinction?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are catalase positive, which separates them from Streptococcus and Enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococci produce catalase, the enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, so mixing a colony with hydrogen peroxide produces visible bubbles. Streptococcus and Enterococcus species do not produce catalase. A positive catalase test therefore places a gram-positive coccus in the genus Staphylococcus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All staphylococci grow in the presence of bile salts, so this result does not sort organisms by genus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulase separates S. aureus from the other staphylococci; it does not sort the genus from streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannitol fermentation on salt agar identifies S. aureus within the staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Novobiocin sensitivity is used to pick out S. saprophyticus among coagulase-negative staphylococci.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man reports a swollen, red bump about 1 inch across on his calf that he thought was a spider bite. There is a pale tan peak at the center that has drained thick exudate, the area is tender and hot, faint red streaking extends proximally, and the inguinal lymph nodes are palpable. Which of the following best describes the lesion and its most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An abscess caused by S. aureus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bullous impetigo caused by S. aureus

explanation.summary: A localized pocket of pus in soft tissue is an abscess, most commonly caused by S. aureus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abscesses are collections of pus in tissues, organs, or other spaces, and S. aureus is the most common cause. They often begin at a trivial break in the skin such as a scratch or an infected hair follicle that was too minor to notice. Management is incision and drainage, with antibiotic coverage that includes MRSA when there is surrounding spread.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bullous impetigo produces fluid-filled blisters on an erythematous base rather than a deep pus collection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. saprophyticus colonizes the urogenital tract and causes urinary infection, not soft tissue abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folliculitis is confined to a hair follicle and appears as a small tender pustule, not a draining pocket of pus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and would not present as a superficial draining skin nodule.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old sexually active woman has 2 days of burning with urination, urinary frequency, and suprapubic pain. She recently returned from her honeymoon. Urine culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative, and resistant to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

explanation.summary: A coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus causing cystitis in a young woman is S. saprophyticus.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. saprophyticus is part of the normal urogenital flora and is the staphylococcus that causes urinary tract infections and cystitis in sexually active young women. Among the staphylococci it is uniquely resistant to novobiocin, and like other coagulase-negative species it fails to clot plasma. Risk factors include sexual activity, a short urethra, and open cuts or sores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecalis is catalase negative and does not form grape-like clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a gram-negative rod and would not appear as gram-positive cocci in clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. aureus is coagulase positive, so the negative coagulase test excludes it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. epidermidis is coagulase negative but is sensitive rather than resistant to novobiocin.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 58-year-old woman with a tunneled central venous catheter develops low-grade fevers. Two blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative, and sensitive to novobiocin. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

explanation.summary: S. epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and the classic pathogen of indwelling catheters.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. epidermidis is a commensal of the skin that is coagulase negative and novobiocin sensitive. It readily colonizes foreign bodies such as central venous catheters and Foley catheters and causes severe endogenous infection in immunosuppressed patients. Its tendency to adhere to plastic surfaces makes catheter-related bloodstream infection its signature presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecalis is catalase negative, so it would not be identified as a staphylococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. aureus clots plasma in the coagulase test and is therefore ruled out.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and is associated with urinary rather than catheter infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus agalactiae is catalase negative and grows in chains rather than clusters.

questions.stem: An isolate of gram-positive cocci in clusters is streaked onto mannitol salt agar. After incubation, the medium surrounding the colonies has turned from red to yellow. This color change is a direct result of which of the following properties of the isolate?

explanation.summary: Yellowing of mannitol salt agar means the organism ferments mannitol, as S. aureus does.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mannitol salt agar contains mannitol plus a pH indicator. S. aureus ferments mannitol and the acid produced turns the agar yellow. Staphylococci that do not ferment mannitol grow as small pink or red colonies and leave the color of the medium unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-hemolysis is clearing of red blood cells on blood agar, a different medium entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Novobiocin resistance is read as growth up to an antibiotic disk rather than as a color change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catalase is detected by bubbling when colonies are mixed with hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coagulase production is detected by clotting plasma in a tube, not by a color change in agar.

questions.stem: Mannitol salt agar is used as a selective medium for gram-positive organisms such as staphylococci. Which component of the medium provides this selectivity?

explanation.summary: Mannitol salt agar for Staphylococcus is selective because of its 7.5% sodium chloride.
explanation.whyCorrect: For Staphylococcus, mannitol salt agar usually contains 7.5% sodium chloride. Most bacteria cannot tolerate that salt concentration, so the medium selects for salt-tolerant gram-positive organisms. The mannitol and pH indicator then differentiate S. aureus, which ferments mannitol and turns the agar yellow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sheep blood is the component of blood agar and is used to read hemolysis patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Novobiocin is applied as a disk in a separate test used to identify S. saprophyticus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bile salts are not the selective agent here, and all staphylococci grow in their presence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydrogen peroxide is the reagent for the catalase test, not a component of the medium.

questions.stem: A catalase-positive, gram-positive coccus that grows in clusters is plated on blood agar and produces colonies surrounded by a clear zone of complete red blood cell lysis. Which of the following additional laboratory results is expected for this isolate?

explanation.summary: Of the main staphylococci, only S. aureus is beta-hemolytic, and only S. aureus is coagulase positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Culturing on blood agar reveals complete lysis of red blood cells by S. aureus, leaving a pale or clear zone around the colonies. S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are nonhemolytic. Because S. aureus is also the only one of the three that produces coagulase, a beta-hemolytic staphylococcus should clot plasma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, are nonhemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. aureus ferments mannitol, which is why it turns mannitol salt agar yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is sensitive to novobiocin; only S. saprophyticus is resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All staphylococci are resistant to bile salts and grow in their presence.

questions.stem: A student is trying to tell apart S. aureus, S. epidermidis, and S. saprophyticus in the laboratory. Which of the following results is identical for all three species and therefore cannot be used to distinguish them?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are bile salt resistant, so that result never distinguishes among the species.
explanation.whyCorrect: All staphylococci grow in the presence of bile salts, so bile salt testing returns the same answer for every species and is useless for separating them. The useful discriminators are coagulase, hemolysis on blood agar, mannitol fermentation, and novobiocin sensitivity. This is why bile salt resistance appears as a uniform row across the identification table.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only S. aureus is beta-hemolytic; the other two are nonhemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only S. aureus produces coagulase, so this test separates it from the other two species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only S. aureus ferments mannitol, turning mannitol salt agar yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant; the other two are sensitive.

questions.stem: An isolate of Staphylococcus grows well both in an aerobic incubator and in an anaerobic jar. Which term best describes this organism's oxygen requirement?

explanation.summary: All staphylococci are facultative anaerobes, capable of both aerobic and anaerobic growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Facultative anaerobes can generate energy with or without oxygen, which is exactly what all staphylococci do. This metabolic flexibility lets them grow on routine laboratory media under either atmosphere and colonize a wide range of body sites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aerotolerant anaerobe survives oxygen but cannot use it, whereas staphylococci grow aerobically.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A microaerophile requires reduced oxygen and grows poorly at atmospheric oxygen levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An obligate aerobe would fail to grow in the anaerobic jar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An obligate anaerobe would fail to grow in the aerobic incubator.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a warm, tender, rapidly spreading area of erythema on the shin that began at a small cut 2 days earlier. The process involves the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and there is no drainable collection of pus. Which term best describes this infection?

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is acute infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually starting at a break in the skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cellulitis is an acute infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues that usually starts from a break in the skin caused by trauma or another infection. It is commonly caused by S. aureus and much less commonly by S. epidermidis. The inflammation is diffuse rather than walled off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abscess is a walled-off collection of pus, which is explicitly absent in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folliculitis is limited to a hair follicle and appears as a small tender pustule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impetigo is a superficial infection with honey-crusted lesions rather than deep spreading erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and would not be diagnosed from spreading skin erythema.

questions.stem: S. aureus produces an enzyme that causes blood clot formation. Which of the following best describes how this enzyme benefits the organism during infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds the Fc portion of IgG, inverting the antibody's orientation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cleaves the beta-lactam ring of penicillin, inactivating the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: It coats the organism in fibrin, shielding it from immune attack

choices.label: D
choices.text: It converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas

choices.label: E
choices.text: It forms pores in leukocyte membranes, killing those cells

explanation.summary: Coagulase builds an insoluble fibrin capsule that hides S. aureus from the immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coagulase causes blood clot formation, and a positive reaction creates an insoluble fibrin capsule around the microorganism. In vivo, that fibrin coat shields the pathogen from the immune response. In the laboratory the same enzyme clots plasma, which is a dead giveaway for S. aureus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That describes protein A, a surface protein that blocks opsonization.
whyWrongByChoice.B: That describes penicillinase, an antibiotic resistance enzyme rather than a clotting enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That describes catalase, which is produced by all staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That describes leukocidin, a pore-forming exotoxin that kills white blood cells.

questions.stem: Protein A is a surface molecule expressed by S. aureus but not by S. epidermidis. Which of the following best describes its action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds the Fc region of IgG and blocks opsonization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converts fibrinogen to fibrin around the bacterial cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forms pores in the membranes of neutrophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Links MHC class II molecules to the T-cell receptor

explanation.summary: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, preventing complement deposition and phagocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protein A binds the Fc region of immunoglobulin G, which inverts the orientation of IgG on the bacterial surface. This both hides bacterial surface antigens and makes the Fc portion unavailable to Fc receptors on phagocytes. The result is inhibited complement deposition and inhibited phagocytosis, leaving S. aureus free to infect cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: That is the action of exfoliatin, which causes blistering skin disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That is the action of coagulase, which builds a fibrin coat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That is the action of leukocidin, a pore-forming exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That is how superantigens such as TSST-1 activate CD4 T cells.

questions.stem: The polysaccharide capsule of S. aureus contributes to virulence primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding the Fc region of IgG on the cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concealing the organism and inhibiting phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converting hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forming pores that kill white blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promoting tissue invasion by destroying host cells

explanation.summary: The S. aureus capsule hides the organism and blocks phagocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The capsule is a polysaccharide covering of S. aureus that hides the organism and inhibits phagocytosis. By preventing phagocytes from engaging the bacterial surface, it allows the organism to survive in tissue. It is one of several S. aureus factors directed at evading the innate immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That is protein A, a distinct surface protein rather than the capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That is catalase, an enzyme that protects against phagocyte killing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: That is leukocidin, a pore-forming exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That is the role of hemolysins, leukotoxins, hyaluronidase, and DNase.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student develops rapidly progressive necrotizing pneumonia, and the S. aureus isolate is found to produce Panton-Valentine leukocidin. The gene encoding this toxin is carried by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacteriophage that infects the bacterium

choices.label: B
choices.text: A plasmid shared with the coagulase gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: A plasmid that also carries the MecA gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The chromosomal gene that encodes protein A

explanation.summary: Leukocidin (PVL) is acquired through a phage, so only some S. aureus strains produce it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocidin is a pore-forming exotoxin that kills white blood cells and causes tissue necrosis, and it is acquired through a phage. Because the gene arrives by bacteriophage rather than being universal to the species, only certain strains of S. aureus carry it. Those PVL-producing strains are the ones capable of causing necrotizing pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulase is produced by essentially all S. aureus strains, whereas leukocidin is strain dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MecA sits on a plasmid and confers methicillin resistance; it does not carry the leukocidin gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gene acquired from enterococci is vanA, which confers vancomycin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein A is a separate virulence factor and is not the vehicle for leukocidin.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 8-year-old girl has 2 days of influenza-like symptoms that abruptly worsen to respiratory failure and septic shock. Sputum culture grows S. aureus. Which bacterial product best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: PVL-producing S. aureus causes necrotizing pneumonia in previously healthy children and young adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strains of S. aureus that produce the pore-forming toxin Panton-Valentine leukocidin can cause necrotizing pneumonia. Previously healthy children or young adults initially present with influenza-like symptoms that rapidly worsen to respiratory failure and septic shock. Mortality is very high unless therapy is started early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsule inhibits phagocytosis but does not destroy lung tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exfoliatin causes blistering skin disease such as bullous impetigo and scalded skin syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterotoxin causes rapid-onset food poisoning with vomiting rather than necrotizing pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TSST causes toxic shock syndrome with fever, hypotension, and a desquamating rash.

questions.stem: A 9-day-old neonate has diffuse erythema with sloughing of the superficial skin over the trunk and neck. Cultures grow S. aureus. The responsible exotoxin produces this lesion by cleaving which of the following?

explanation.summary: Exfoliatin cleaves desmoglein-1, splitting the epidermis just below the stratum corneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exfoliatin, also called exfoliative toxin, is a proteolytic exotoxin that cleaves desmoglein-1, an adhesion molecule of desmosomes. Loss of that adhesion produces a blister just below the stratum corneum of the epidermal skin. This is the mechanism behind both staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and bullous impetigo.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulase acts on fibrinogen to create a fibrin coat around the organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaluronidase degrades connective tissue to promote invasion but does not split the epidermis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vanA gene product alters muramic acid side chains to resist vancomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillinase cleaves the beta-lactam ring, an antibiotic resistance mechanism.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has red sores around her nose and mouth that began as small red spots and have progressed to clear, fluid-filled bullae surrounded by crusted erythematous lesions. Which S. aureus product accounts for the bullae?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superantigen activation of CD4 T cells

explanation.summary: Bullous impetigo is impetigo caused by an exfoliative toxin-producing strain of S. aureus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impetigo is a common superficial skin infection with highly contagious honey-crusted lesions usually caused by S. aureus. When the strain produces exfoliative toxin, fluid-filled bullae form at the site of infection, which is bullous impetigo. Strains that do not make the toxin still cause impetigo but do not produce blisters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biofilm formation is a feature of S. epidermidis on medical devices and does not blister skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Novobiocin resistance is a laboratory identification feature of S. saprophyticus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein A blocks opsonization but does not separate epidermal layers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigen activation drives toxic shock syndrome with a diffuse rash, not localized bullae.

questions.stem: A patient with staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome has fever, hypotension, and a diffuse rash driven by massive release of IFN-gamma, IL-1-beta, and TNF-alpha. Which mechanism best explains this cytokine surge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The toxin binds the Fc region of IgG and triggers complement activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The toxin cleaves desmosomal proteins and releases inflammatory mediators

choices.label: C
choices.text: The toxin coats the organism with fibrin, trapping inflammatory cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The toxin forms pores in leukocytes, spilling their cytokine stores

choices.label: E
choices.text: The toxin links MHC class II to the T-cell receptor without a bound peptide

explanation.summary: TSST-1 is a superantigen that bridges MHC class II and the T-cell receptor without antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Superantigens facilitate binding of MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells to the T-cell receptor of CD4 T cells. This interaction occurs without a peptide in the T-cell receptor groove, so enormous numbers of T cells are activated non-specifically. The resulting significant release of cytokines produces the shock and multiorgan failure of TSS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding the Fc region of IgG is protein A, which inhibits rather than amplifies the immune response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleaving desmosomal proteins is the action of exfoliatin, which causes blistering skin disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin coating is the action of coagulase, an immune evasion rather than activation strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pore formation is the mechanism of leukocidin, which kills white blood cells rather than activating them.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman develops fever to 39.4 C, blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg, vomiting, and a diffuse erythematous rash on the trunk 3 days after nasal packing was placed following sinus surgery. Examination shows conjunctival hyperemia and a strawberry tongue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic shock syndrome due to TSST

explanation.summary: TSS is classically linked to tampon use and foreign bodies such as postoperative nasal packing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Toxic shock syndrome is associated with tampon use and with foreign bodies such as nasal packing following surgery. It presents with fever, hypotension with dizziness and multiorgan failure, nausea and vomiting, and a diffuse erythema that starts on the trunk with conjunctival hyperemia and strawberry tongue. Any S. aureus infection can potentially lead to TSS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute endocarditis presents with a new murmur and valvular vegetations, not a diffuse erythematous rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Necrotizing pneumonia presents with respiratory failure following influenza-like symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Food poisoning from enterotoxin causes vomiting within hours of a meal, without shock or rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scalded skin syndrome causes sloughing of superficial skin rather than hypotension with strawberry tongue.

questions.stem: A patient recovers from staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome with supportive care. Which finding is most likely to appear 1 to 2 weeks after the acute illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tender pustule forming at each hair follicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deep abscesses appearing in the extremities

choices.label: C
choices.text: Desquamation of the rash on the palms and soles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Honey-colored crusts forming over the face

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tense bullae developing across the trunk

explanation.summary: The TSS rash desquamates 1 to 2 weeks after onset, especially on the palms and soles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rash of toxic shock syndrome begins as diffuse erythema on the trunk that spreads to the extremities, with erythema of the palms and soles. One to two weeks later the rash desquamates, particularly on the palms and soles. This delayed peeling is a characteristic feature that supports the diagnosis in retrospect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Follicular pustules define folliculitis, an infection of the hair follicle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abscesses are localized pus collections and are not the expected sequel of the TSS rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Honey-colored crusting is the lesion of impetigo, a localized superficial skin infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tense bullae characterize bullous impetigo and scalded skin syndrome, which are caused by exfoliatin.

questions.stem: Four people become ill 3 hours after a picnic at which potato salad was served. All have prominent nausea and vomiting, some have watery diarrhea, none are febrile, and all recover within a day. Which of the following best explains the illness?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ingestion of preformed enterotoxin in the food

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasion of enterocytes by S. aureus after ingestion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Superantigen released from an unrecognized skin abscess

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxin made by S. aureus colonizing the colon

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal enterotoxin causes food poisoning with symptoms 1 to 6 hours after ingestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterotoxin causes rapid-onset food poisoning, with symptoms arising within 1 to 6 hours of ingesting contaminated food. Nausea and vomiting predominate, and watery diarrhea may also occur. The toxin is already present in the food, so illness does not require the bacteria to grow in the gut.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacteremia would produce fever and systemic illness rather than a self-limited day of vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcal food poisoning is toxin mediated, and 3-hour onset is far too fast for invasive infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The shared meal with simultaneous onset in four people points to contaminated food, not a skin lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxin produced after colonization of the colon would take much longer than 3 hours to cause symptoms.

questions.stem: Leftover food from a gathering is thoroughly reheated to boiling before being served again, yet several people who eat it still develop vomiting within a few hours. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reheating converts the toxin into a more active form

choices.label: B
choices.text: S. aureus multiplies faster than heating can kill it

choices.label: C
choices.text: Staphylococcal spores survive boiling and germinate in the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enterotoxin is heat resistant and stable at 100 C for 1 hour

choices.label: E
choices.text: The toxin is produced only after the food has been eaten

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal enterotoxin is heat resistant, remaining stable at 100 C for an hour.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterotoxin is heat resistant and stable at 100 C for 1 hour. Reheating kills the bacteria but leaves the preformed toxin intact, so the food still causes rapid-onset vomiting. This illustrates the general principle that exotoxin-mediated effects persist even when the organism is eliminated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heating does not activate the toxin; the toxin is already active and simply survives heating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Boiling does kill S. aureus; the problem is the toxin left behind, not continued bacterial growth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococci are non-spore-forming, so there are no spores to survive boiling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The toxin is preformed in the food, which is why symptoms begin within 1 to 6 hours.

questions.stem: A laboratory screens purified S. aureus products for the ability to activate large numbers of CD4 T cells without processed antigen. Which pair of products would be expected to show this activity?

explanation.summary: TSST-1 and enterotoxin are both superantigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Superantigens activate T cells by linking MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells directly to the T-cell receptor without a peptide in the receptor groove. TSST-1 and enterotoxin are both superantigens, which is why each can drive a systemic cytokine-mediated illness. The resulting cytokine release accounts for shock in severe cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide and exfoliatin splits the epidermis; neither is a superantigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterotoxin is a superantigen, but exfoliatin is a protease that cleaves desmoglein-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TSST-1 is a superantigen, but leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that kills leukocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein A blocks opsonization and coagulase forms fibrin; neither activates T cells.

questions.stem: An infection control team wants to screen health care workers for S. aureus carriage. Which body site is most commonly colonized by this organism?

explanation.summary: S. aureus is most commonly found as normal flora in the anterior nares.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. aureus can be part of the normal flora of human skin, but it is most commonly found as normal flora in the anterior nares. Transient colonization of moist skin folds and the nasopharyngeal cavity is also common. S. aureus can additionally survive for long periods on dry surfaces, which supports spread by fomites.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The conjunctiva is not a described colonization site for staphylococci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The distal urethra is not the classic staphylococcal carriage site; S. saprophyticus favors the urogenital tract.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The external ear canal is not the site used for S. aureus carriage screening.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The gingival crevice is not described as a typical staphylococcal niche.

questions.stem: S. saprophyticus is part of the normal flora at which of the following sites, where it is present in up to 10% of females?

explanation.summary: S. saprophyticus is normal vaginal flora in up to 10% of females and colonizes the urogenital tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. saprophyticus is part of the normal vaginal flora and is present in up to 10% of females. From this urogenital reservoir it reaches the bladder and causes cystitis, with dysuria, polyuria, and abdominal or suprapubic pain. Diagnosis rests on urinalysis and culture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anterior nares are the classic reservoir of S. aureus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Axillary skin is a general staphylococcal niche, not the specific reservoir for S. saprophyticus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The large intestine is not the reservoir described for S. saprophyticus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oropharynx is not described as a colonization site for this organism.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a chronically infected prosthetic knee. Cultures repeatedly grow S. epidermidis despite prolonged antibiotic therapy. Which property of this organism best accounts for its persistence on the implant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fermentation of mannitol within the joint

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of a biofilm on the device surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of coagulase around the implant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of exfoliative toxin into the joint

explanation.summary: S. epidermidis forms biofilms on prosthetic material, which resist antibiotics and immune clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. epidermidis is very good at generating biofilms, microbial communities embedded in a matrix on a surface. Biofilms increase antimicrobial resistance, promote immune evasion, and allow colonies to break off and disseminate. This is why S. epidermidis is the classic pathogen of prosthetic joints, prosthetic heart valves, and indwelling urinary catheters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: S. epidermidis does not ferment mannitol, and mannitol fermentation plays no role in device infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. epidermidis is coagulase negative and does not produce this enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Novobiocin resistance belongs to S. saprophyticus and is an identification feature, not a persistence mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exfoliative toxin is an S. aureus product that causes blistering skin disease.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman develops low-grade fever and fatigue 5 months after mechanical aortic valve replacement. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the prosthetic valve, and blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve endocarditis in the first year after surgery is almost exclusively S. epidermidis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prosthetic valve endocarditis during the initial year after surgery is almost exclusively caused by S. epidermidis, which forms a biofilm on the implanted material. Subacute endocarditis in patients with heart defects or valve replacements is usually caused by this organism and may produce few to no symptoms. The indolent low-grade fever and fatigue here are typical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecalis is catalase negative and would not be described as staphylococcal clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. aureus causes acute endocarditis with large vegetations on native valves, classically with injection drug use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is a urinary pathogen and is not associated with prosthetic valve infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes grows in chains and is catalase negative.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man who injects heroin with nonsterile equipment presents with high fever and a new murmur. Echocardiography shows large vegetations on a previously normal tricuspid valve. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Acute endocarditis with tricuspid vegetations in an injection drug user is most often S. aureus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute endocarditis involves large vegetations on both normal and diseased heart valves, most commonly affects the tricuspid valve, and is most often seen with unsterile intravenous drug use. S. aureus is the most common cause of acute cases. This contrasts with the subacute, prosthetic-valve disease caused by S. epidermidis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutibacterium is an anaerobic gram-positive rod, not a cause of acute tricuspid endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterococcus faecalis is not the organism most often implicated in acute injection-related endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. epidermidis causes subacute endocarditis on abnormal or replaced valves, not acute disease on normal valves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. saprophyticus causes urinary tract infection and is not an endocarditis pathogen.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has fever and point tenderness over the distal femur, and MRI shows marrow changes consistent with osteomyelitis. Which organism is the most common cause of this infection?

explanation.summary: Many organisms cause osteomyelitis, but S. aureus is the most common.
explanation.whyCorrect: Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone, and although many organisms can cause it, S. aureus is the most common. The organism reaches bone by extension from soft tissue infection or by hematogenous spread. S. aureus is likewise the leading staphylococcal cause of cellulitis, abscesses, and septic arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E. coli is a gram-negative rod and is not the leading cause of osteomyelitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. epidermidis causes osteomyelitis mainly around joint replacement hardware, not spontaneously in a healthy child.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is confined largely to urinary tract disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes is not the most common cause of osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man recovering from influenza suddenly worsens on day 6 with high fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation. Sputum Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Post-influenza secondary pneumonia is the classic way S. aureus causes community-acquired pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary pneumonia occurs as a result of another illness such as influenza or cystic fibrosis, and this is the most common way S. aureus causes community-acquired pneumonia. S. aureus should be considered during influenza epidemics or when there is a recent history of viral pneumonia. Gram-positive cocci in clusters on sputum Gram stain support the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cutibacterium is an anaerobic gram-positive rod, not a coccus in clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. epidermidis is a device-associated pathogen and does not typically cause post-influenza pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is a urinary pathogen with no role in pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes forms chains rather than clusters on Gram stain.

questions.stem: S. aureus is estimated to cause what proportion of health care-associated pneumonias?

explanation.summary: S. aureus causes an estimated 20% to 50% of health care-associated pneumonias.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. aureus is estimated to cause 20% to 50% of health care-associated pneumonias, a much larger share than its contribution to community-acquired disease. It is most commonly acquired in the hospital, especially by patients who have been on a ventilator. Ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia is one of its classic nosocomial presentations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% to 10% is the estimated share of community-acquired pneumonias caused by S. aureus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Less than 1% badly underestimates the role of S. aureus in hospital-acquired pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 40% is the share of health care-associated S. aureus infections that are methicillin resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: More than 75% overstates the share; no single organism dominates to that degree.

questions.stem: Most S. aureus strains are resistant to conventional penicillin. The enzyme responsible for this resistance acts in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alters the muramic acid side chain, causing steric hindrance

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cleaves the beta-lactam ring of penicillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It degrades the peptidoglycan that the drug targets

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces an altered penicillin-binding protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: It pumps the drug out of the bacterial cell

explanation.summary: Penicillinase cleaves the beta-lactam ring, inactivating conventional penicillin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most S. aureus strains are resistant to conventional penicillin because they produce the penicillinase enzyme. Bacterial penicillinase cleaves the beta-lactam ring of penicillin, which makes the drug ineffective. This mechanism is separate from methicillin resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altering the muramic acid side chain is how the vanA gene confers vancomycin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillinase attacks the antibiotic itself, not the bacterium's own peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Altered penicillin-binding proteins are encoded by MecA and explain methicillin resistance, not penicillinase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Efflux is not the mechanism described for staphylococcal penicillin resistance.

questions.stem: An S. aureus blood isolate is reported as methicillin resistant and is also resistant to nearly all other beta-lactam antibiotics. This broad resistance is conferred by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacteriophage carrying the leukocidin gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chromosomal gene for capsular polysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: MecA, which encodes altered penicillin-binding proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vanA gene acquired from enterococcal strains

explanation.summary: MRSA resistance comes from altered penicillin-binding proteins encoded by the MecA gene.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methicillin resistance, along with resistance to almost all other drugs containing a beta-lactam ring, is conferred by altered penicillin-binding proteins. Those altered proteins are encoded by the MecA gene, which is found on a plasmid. MRSA accounts for about 40% of all health care-associated S. aureus infections in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The leukocidin phage carries a tissue-destroying toxin and plays no role in antibiotic resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The capsule inhibits phagocytosis and does not affect antibiotic susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillinase explains resistance to conventional penicillin, but methicillin was designed to resist that enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: vanA confers vancomycin resistance rather than beta-lactam resistance.

questions.stem: A rare S. aureus isolate has a vancomycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 32 micrograms/mL. The gene responsible was acquired from which organism, and what does it alter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From a bacteriophage; it forms membrane pores

choices.label: B
choices.text: From Clostridium; it cleaves the beta-lactam ring

choices.label: C
choices.text: From Enterococcus; it alters penicillin-binding proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: From Enterococcus; it alters the muramic acid side chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: From Streptococcus; it alters penicillin-binding proteins

explanation.summary: VRSA strains acquired vanA from enterococci, which changes the muramic acid side chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus strains acquired the vanA gene from enterococci, a remarkable example of genetic transmission between bacterial genera. The vanA gene changes the amino acids on the muramic acid side chain, causing steric hindrance that decreases the ability of vancomycin to bind. Only a handful of VRSA infections have been reported in the United States since the first case in 2002.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A phage carries the leukocidin gene, which forms pores in leukocytes rather than conferring resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clostridium is not the source, and beta-lactam ring cleavage is the action of penicillinase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The source organism is right, but vanA alters the muramic acid side chain, not penicillin-binding proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The source is enterococci, and altered penicillin-binding proteins mediate beta-lactam rather than vancomycin resistance.

questions.stem: A clinical laboratory reports a vancomycin minimum inhibitory concentration of 6 micrograms/mL for an S. aureus blood isolate. How should this isolate be classified?

explanation.summary: A vancomycin MIC of 4 to 8 micrograms/mL defines VISA; 16 or higher defines VRSA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococci are classified as VISA when the vancomycin minimum inhibitory concentration is 4 to 8 micrograms/mL, and an MIC of 6 falls in that range. The MIC is the standard measure used to determine whether an organism is resistant to an antimicrobial being considered for treatment. Classification as VRSA requires an MIC of 16 micrograms/mL or higher.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An MIC in the 4 to 8 range is above the fully susceptible range and defines intermediate status.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methicillin resistance is determined by beta-lactam testing, not by the vancomycin MIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillinase production is inferred from penicillin resistance and is unrelated to the vancomycin MIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VRSA requires a vancomycin MIC of 16 micrograms/mL or higher.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has a purulent wound. Gram stain of the drainage shows gram-positive cocci. When a drop of hydrogen peroxide is added to a colony from the blood agar plate, no bubbling is observed. This test result is most useful for distinguishing the isolate from which of the following organisms?

explanation.summary: The catalase test separates catalase-negative streptococci and enterococci from catalase-positive staphylococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are gram-positive, nonmotile, non-spore-forming and uniformly catalase negative. Staphylococci produce catalase, which liberates oxygen bubbles from hydrogen peroxide. A negative catalase test therefore argues against Staphylococcus aureus and supports a streptococcal or enterococcal isolate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus species are also catalase negative, so the test cannot separate them from streptococci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Streptococcus agalactiae is catalase negative and would also fail to bubble.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae is catalase negative and is not distinguished by this test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus pyogenes is catalase negative and would give this same result.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-positive cocci arranged in pairs, with each coccus having a pointed, lancet-shaped end. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci are the classic morphology of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. pneumoniae is described as having a lancet-shaped appearance: the diplococci have a pointed end on each coccus. It is a leading cause of meningitis, and its capsule allows it to spread systemically and cross the blood-brain barrier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Staphylococcus aureus forms grape-like clusters, not pairs in chains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae appears in chains and is a neonatal rather than elderly meningitis pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mutans is a viridans streptococcus that appears in chains and causes dental caries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes appears in chains rather than as lancet-shaped pairs.

questions.stem: A throat swab from a 9-year-old with a sore throat is plated on blood agar. After overnight incubation the colonies are surrounded by a completely clear, transparent zone where the red blood cells have been destroyed. Gram stain shows cocci in chains. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Complete (beta) hemolysis on blood agar points to S. pyogenes or S. agalactiae; in a pharyngitis case it is S. pyogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are divided by how readily they lyse red blood cells. Beta hemolysis is complete destruction of RBCs, leaving a clear halo around the colony, and S. pyogenes and S. agalactiae are the beta-hemolytic species. S. pyogenes colonizes the skin and throat and is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus species are gamma-hemolytic (or alpha), leaving red blood cells intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. gallolyticus subspecies generally demonstrate gamma hemolysis (nonhemolytic).
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mitis is a viridans streptococcus and is alpha-hemolytic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic aerobically, producing partial green discoloration rather than a clear zone.

questions.stem: Two beta-hemolytic streptococcal isolates are tested with a bacitracin disk. Isolate 1 shows a clear zone of inhibition around the disk; isolate 2 grows right up to the edge of the disk. Which of the following statements best interprets these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both isolates belong to Lancefield group B

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. agalactiae and isolate 2 is S. pyogenes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. pneumoniae and isolate 2 is S. mitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolate 1 is S. pyogenes and isolate 2 is S. agalactiae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither isolate can be assigned a Lancefield group

explanation.summary: Group A streptococci are bacitracin sensitive; group B streptococci are bacitracin resistant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacitracin is a polypeptide antibiotic that interferes with peptidoglycan synthesis. Group A streptococci such as S. pyogenes are inhibited by only a small amount of bacitracin, whereas group B streptococci such as S. agalactiae usually are not. The mnemonic B-BRAS captures this: group B strep are Resistant, group A strep are Sensitive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the bacitracin-resistant isolate fits group B; the sensitive one is group A.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the relationship; group B strep are the resistant organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. pneumoniae and S. mitis are alpha-hemolytic and are separated by optochin, not bacitracin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-hemolytic streptococci are precisely the group that is further classified by Lancefield grouping.

questions.stem: Sputum from a patient with lobar pneumonia grows an alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive coccus. Growth of the isolate is reliably inhibited around an optochin disk. Which of the following organisms is most likely?

explanation.summary: Optochin sensitivity separates S. pneumoniae from the other alpha-hemolytic streptococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: Optochin reliably inhibits the growth of S. pneumoniae on culture plates, while viridans and other streptococci are optochin resistant. S. pneumoniae is also the most common cause of bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which fits the clinical picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus faecium is gamma-hemolytic and is identified by growth in 6.5% NaCl.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae is beta-hemolytic and bacitracin resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mutans is a viridans streptococcus and is optochin resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic and is identified with the bacitracin disk.

questions.stem: An alpha-hemolytic gram-positive coccus is recovered from blood cultures. A turbid suspension of the organism is mixed with bile, and the turbidity clears. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The isolate belongs to Lancefield group A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The isolate is a viridans group streptococcus

choices.label: C
choices.text: The isolate is beta-hemolytic when grown aerobically

explanation.summary: Bile solubility distinguishes bile-soluble S. pneumoniae from the bile-insoluble viridans streptococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bile solubility test distinguishes bile-soluble S. pneumoniae from all other alpha-hemolytic (viridans) streptococci, which are bile insoluble. A clearing of the turbidity in the bile tube indicates a positive test, meaning the organism has lysed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lancefield grouping is applied to beta-hemolytic streptococci, not to this alpha-hemolytic isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viridans group streptococci are bile insoluble, so the tube would remain turbid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic in aerobic conditions and beta-hemolytic only anaerobically.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clearing of the tube defines a positive test, meaning the organism is bile soluble.

questions.stem: A reference laboratory types several beta-hemolytic streptococcal isolates using panels of specific antisera, assigning each isolate to a letter group. The serologic scheme these antisera rely on is based primarily on antigenic differences in which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzymatic hydrolysis of the PYR substrate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Susceptibility to optochin and to bacitracin

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ability to grow in 6.5% sodium chloride

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hemolysins released onto blood agar

explanation.summary: Lancefield grouping is a serologic scheme based on surface antigens, chiefly cell wall carbohydrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Streptococci are subdivided by antibodies that recognize surface antigens into Lancefield groups, which may include one or more species. Grouping is based on antigenic differences in cell wall carbohydrates (groups A to V), in cell wall pili-associated protein, and in the polysaccharide capsule in group B streptococci.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The PYR test is a biochemical assay for a specific enzyme, not an antigen-antibody reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Optochin and bacitracin susceptibility are physiologic tests, not serologic grouping.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Salt tolerance is a biochemical test used to separate Enterococcus from nonenterococcal group D organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysin activity defines the alpha, beta, and gamma hemolytic patterns, a separate classification method.

questions.stem: A urine culture from a hospitalized 71-year-old man grows a catalase-negative, gamma-hemolytic gram-positive coccus. When the isolate is tested with the pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) reagent, the reagent turns cherry-red. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: A positive PYR test narrows a gram-positive coccus to S. pyogenes or Enterococcus; gamma hemolysis then points to Enterococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PYR test is used for presumptive identification of S. pyogenes and Enterococcus spp.; hydrolysis of the substrate turns the reagent pink or cherry-red. Since this isolate is gamma-hemolytic rather than beta-hemolytic, it is an Enterococcus, and enterococci commonly cause urinary tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S. agalactiae is beta-hemolytic and is not a PYR-positive organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. gallolyticus is gamma-hemolytic but is not identified by a positive PYR reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. mitis is an alpha-hemolytic viridans streptococcus of the oral cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and is identified by optochin sensitivity and bile solubility.

questions.stem: Two nonhemolytic, catalase-negative gram-positive cocci are recovered from separate blood cultures. Both organisms grow in the presence of bile, but only isolate B also grows in broth containing 6.5% sodium chloride. Isolate B is best identified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Both group D strep and enterococci grow in bile, but only Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterococcus spp. are very similar to group D strep such as S. gallolyticus but can be distinguished by their ability to grow in salt. Both S. gallolyticus and Enterococcus spp. grow in bile, but only Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl media. E. faecalis and E. faecium are nonhemolytic and are the two named species.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S. gallolyticus grows in bile but does not tolerate 6.5% NaCl, matching isolate A instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. mitis is an alpha-hemolytic viridans streptococcus, not a salt-tolerant nonhemolytic organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and bile soluble rather than nonhemolytic and salt tolerant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pyogenes is beta-hemolytic and would not be described as nonhemolytic.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has 2 days of sore throat and malaise. Her temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), her pharynx is erythematous with enlarged tonsils, and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. She has no cough, rhinorrhea, or conjunctivitis. Which of the following features most strongly supports a bacterial rather than a viral cause of her pharyngitis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The absence of any measurable fever

explanation.summary: Fever plus cervical adenopathy without upper respiratory symptoms favors streptococcal pharyngitis over a viral cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. pyogenes is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis, and patients present with a combination of fever, malaise, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Viruses are by far the most common cause of pharyngitis overall, but they usually present without fever or adenopathy and with other respiratory symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjunctivitis is one of the upper respiratory findings that suggests a viral cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lower respiratory tract symptoms accompany viral pharyngitis rather than GAS infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rhinorrhea and cough are viral features rather than features of strep throat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lack of fever is characteristic of viral pharyngitis, not streptococcal disease.

questions.stem: A child with fever and a sore throat has a rapid strep test performed on a throat swab in clinic. A visible line appears within minutes, confirming the diagnosis. This point-of-care assay detects which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysin released onto a blood agar plate

explanation.summary: The rapid strep test is an antibody-based immunoassay for the group A carbohydrate antigen on a throat swab.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the clinic, the rapid antigen detection test for strep detects S. pyogenes by identifying the group-specific carbohydrate antigen in a throat swab using antibody-based immunoassay technology. A visible line indicates a positive result within minutes, which is very useful for confirming a diagnosis of strep throat.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Streptococci are catalase negative, so catalase activity is not the target of this assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysin activity is assessed by culture on blood agar, not by a swab-based strip test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-streptolysin O titers document a recent infection serologically, not an acute throat swab result.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rapid test described uses immunoassay technology rather than nucleic acid amplification.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has several crusted lesions on his chin and around his nose. The lesions are erythematous and covered with a honey-colored crust; no blisters are present. Nonbullous impetigo is diagnosed. Although S. pyogenes can produce these lesions, which of the following organisms is the most common cause of both nonbullous and bullous impetigo?

explanation.summary: Impetigo caused by S. pyogenes is nonbullous, but S. aureus is the most common cause of impetigo overall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impetigo is an epidermal skin infection producing crusted lesions at the site of inoculation, and impetigo caused by S. pyogenes is specifically nonbullous (nonblistering). Staphylococcus aureus, however, is the most common cause of both nonbullous and bullous impetigo.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococci cause endocarditis, urinary, biliary, and wound infections rather than impetigo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. agalactiae colonizes the vagina and GI tract and causes neonatal invasive disease, not impetigo.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. mutans is an oral organism that causes dental caries and subacute endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes respiratory and systemic infections rather than crusted skin lesions.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man develops a bright red, swollen, painful patch on his cheek over 24 hours. The lesion has a raised, indurated, sharply demarcated border, and point pain is prominent. Which of the following best describes the anatomic location of this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deep fascia, with rapid tissue necrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dermis and the subcutaneous layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: The epidermis at the site of inoculation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pharyngeal mucosa and the tonsils

choices.label: E
choices.text: The upper dermis and superficial lymphatics

explanation.summary: Erysipelas is a S. pyogenes infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics with a raised, well-demarcated border.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erysipelas causes local redness and swelling of the skin with a characteristic raised, indurated border, and point pain is common. It is distinguished from cellulitis, which is an even deeper S. pyogenes infection of the dermis and subcutaneous layer with ill-defined borders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deep fascial involvement describes necrotizing fasciitis, which is far more severe and rapidly progressive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The dermis and subcutaneous layer describe cellulitis, which has ill-defined rather than sharp borders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An epidermal infection at an inoculation site describes impetigo with its honey-colored crust.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pharyngeal mucosal infection describes streptococcal pharyngitis, not a facial skin lesion.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with untreated streptococcal pharyngitis develops a diffuse, confluent erythematous rash with a fine sandpaper-like texture that blanches with pressure. It began on the chest and neck and spread outward, sparing the nasolabial triangle and chin. His tongue is bright red with hyperplastic papillae. Which of the following findings is most likely to develop next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crepitus palpable over the affected skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fine desquamation of the fingers in week two

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypotension progressing to shock over hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints

explanation.summary: Scarlet fever produces a blanching sandpaper rash with circumoral pallor that later desquamates, beginning at the fingers.
explanation.whyCorrect: In scarlet fever, a systemic release of erythrogenic toxins produces a confluent, sandpaper-like blanching rash that begins on the chest and neck and spreads outward, along with circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue. Rashes may be followed by fine desquamation (peeling) starting with the fingers in the second week.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crepitus from gas-producing bacteria is a sign of necrotizing fasciitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypotension with shock is the defining feature of toxic shock-like syndrome, not scarlet fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Migratory polyarthritis is a major Jones criterion of rheumatic fever, which follows weeks later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nephritic urine and edema describe poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, a later immune-complex sequela.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation has a routine screening culture that is positive for vaginal colonization with Streptococcus agalactiae. She has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to reduce the risk of invasive disease in her newborn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic treatment of the infant at 6 weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cesarean delivery to bypass the birth canal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal vaccination in the third trimester

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral antibiotics started right after delivery

explanation.summary: Universal GBS screening in pregnancy is followed by intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in colonized mothers.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. agalactiae is normal flora of the vagina and gastrointestinal tract and is most commonly transmitted via the birth canal, with risk increasing after prolonged membrane rupture. Universal screening for vaginal colonization is recommended, and if a pregnant person tests positive, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is given during labor, which drastically reduces invasive neonatal disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neonatal GBS disease occurs in the first weeks of life, especially the first week, so 6 weeks is far too late.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prevention rests on antibiotic prophylaxis during labor rather than on operative delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A maternal GBS vaccine is not part of the described prevention strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treating after delivery is too late, since transmission occurs as the infant passes through the birth canal.

questions.stem: A strain of S. pyogenes isolated from a patient with scarlet fever produces streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A (SPE-A), whereas an otherwise similar strain from a patient with uncomplicated pharyngitis does not. The genes encoding SPE-A and SPE-C are most likely acquired by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spontaneous point mutation of a capsular gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transposition of a chromosomal insertion element

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uptake of naked DNA released by lysed cells

explanation.summary: The erythrogenic toxins SPE-A and SPE-C are phage-encoded and reach S. pyogenes by lysogenic conversion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Toxigenic infections such as scarlet fever, toxic shock-like syndrome, and necrotizing fasciitis are caused by toxins produced by S. pyogenes. The erythrogenic toxins SPE-A and SPE-C are transmitted to S. pyogenes by bacteriophages via lysogenic conversion, which is why only some strains carry them.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasmid conjugation is not the described route of acquisition for these exotoxin genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A point mutation in a capsule gene would not create a new exotoxin gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Movement of a chromosomal insertion sequence does not introduce new toxin genes from outside the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transformation by naked DNA is not how these phage-borne toxin genes are described as spreading.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a painful cellulitis of the forearm becomes acutely ill with a temperature of 39.5 C, a diffuse rash, and a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow S. pyogenes. Which of the following features most clearly distinguishes his illness from scarlet fever?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A diffuse rash that later desquamates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fever accompanying the onset of rash

explanation.summary: Hypotension, potentially with shock, is the defining feature of toxic shock-like syndrome that scarlet fever lacks.
explanation.whyCorrect: In toxic shock-like syndrome, systemic release of SPE-A from a S. pyogenes cellulitis causes polyclonal T-cell activation with acute fever and shock, and patients have painful preexisting skin infections and positive blood cultures. Like scarlet fever, a diffuse rash with subsequent peeling may occur, but hypotension, potentially with shock, is a defining characteristic of TSLS that is not present in scarlet fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A diffuse rash with later peeling occurs in both scarlet fever and TSLS, so it does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both syndromes follow a S. pyogenes infection, pharyngeal in scarlet fever and cutaneous in TSLS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fever is present in both toxin-mediated syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both illnesses are driven by erythrogenic exotoxins produced by S. pyogenes.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes has a rapidly enlarging violaceous patch on his thigh with tense bullae and sloughing skin. He initially had pain far out of proportion to his physical findings, but the pain has now lessened. Crepitus is palpable at the margin. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral antibiotics with outpatient wound checks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeat examination in 24 hours before treating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Topical antibiotic ointment and dry dressings

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urgent surgical debridement and IV antibiotics

explanation.summary: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring prompt debridement plus empiric IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of the deep fascia and subcutaneous tissues. Patients often have severe pain disproportionate to physical findings that may diminish as the infection damages sensory nerves, and crepitus may be heard from gas-producing bacteria. It is a surgical emergency requiring prompt surgical debridement and empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral therapy alone cannot control a rapidly progressive deep fascial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delaying treatment for 24 hours is dangerous in a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topical therapy does not reach the deep fascia where the infection resides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supportive measures without surgery allow the necrotizing process to advance.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl had streptococcal pharyngitis treated with only three doses of amoxicillin. Nearly 4 weeks later she has fevers above 39 C, migratory joint pain that has moved from her left knee and hip to her right knee and hip, chest pain, and a new heart murmur. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of her current illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody cross-reactivity between M protein and myosin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the cardiac myocardium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythrogenic toxin damage to the cardiac valve leaflets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in glomerular capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superantigen-driven polyclonal activation of T cells

explanation.summary: Rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity driven by molecular mimicry between S. pyogenes M protein and host proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatic fever is a type II hypersensitivity reaction triggered by cross-reactivity between S. pyogenes antigens such as M protein and host cardiac, joint, and neuronal proteins such as myosin. It typically develops 2-3 weeks after an episode of untreated streptococcal pharyngitis, especially in children, who account for about 80% of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Rheumatic carditis is immune-mediated rather than the result of direct bacterial invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythrogenic toxins cause scarlet fever; valve injury here is due to cross-reactive antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition describes poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, a type III reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polyclonal T-cell activation by superantigens causes toxic shock-like syndrome, not rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy has an elevated anti-streptolysin O titer documenting a recent group A streptococcal infection. On examination, his only major manifestation is carditis, evidenced by a new murmur. Which of the following additional findings would satisfy the diagnostic criteria for acute rheumatic fever?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An anti-DNase B titer repeated in two weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arthralgia counted while polyarthritis is evident

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fever plus a prolonged PR interval on ECG

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three minor findings without any major finding

explanation.summary: Rheumatic fever requires evidence of recent GAS infection plus two major Jones criteria or one major and two minor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis requires evidence of a recent GAS infection (serology from ASO titer or anti-DNase B) together with either two major Jones criteria or one major and two minor criteria. Minor criteria include fever, arthralgia, increased acute phase reactants such as CRP or ESR, and a prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram. Carditis plus fever and a prolonged PR interval is one major plus two minor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Repeat serology confirms recent infection, which is already established, and adds no criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Arthralgia cannot be used as a criterion if polyarthritis is evident.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single major manifestation alone does not meet the criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Minor criteria alone are insufficient; at least one major criterion is required.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought in with dark, tea-colored urine, periorbital edema, and hypertension. Two weeks earlier he had crusted skin lesions diagnosed as impetigo, for which he completed a full course of antibiotics. Which of the following best explains his current findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct streptococcal invasion of the renal tubules

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgA protease cleavage of antibody in the glomerulus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Superantigen-driven cytokine release within the kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type II hypersensitivity against glomerular basement membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type III hypersensitivity with immune complex deposition

explanation.summary: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex (type III) disease that can follow skin or throat infection even after treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that can follow skin or pharyngeal streptococcal infections even if antibiotic treatment was administered. Circulating immune complex deposition causes glomerular damage and subsequent nephritic syndrome, and diagnosis can be made with elevated ASO or anti-DNase B titers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The glomerular injury is immune mediated, not the result of bacteria invading the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA protease is a S. pneumoniae virulence factor acting on mucosal antibody, not a cause of nephritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Superantigen-driven cytokine release produces toxic shock-like syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type II antibody-mediated cross-reactivity describes rheumatic fever, not PSGN.

questions.stem: A research group compares wild-type S. pyogenes with a mutant lacking a surface protein that exists in more than 100 immunotypes. The mutant is readily ingested by neutrophils in serum, whereas the wild type is not. Which of the following best describes how this surface protein contributes to virulence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks complement, inhibiting opsonization and phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It converts plasminogen to plasmin, producing fibrinolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links T-cell receptors and MHC II nonspecifically

choices.label: D
choices.text: It degrades connective tissue to allow spread through tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: It forms an antiphagocytic layer of hyaluronic acid

explanation.summary: M protein is the antiphagocytic S. pyogenes surface protein that blocks complement and drives rheumatic fever by mimicry.
explanation.whyCorrect: M protein, which exists in more than 100 immunotypes, acts to inhibit opsonization and phagocytosis by blocking complement. The host immune response to it can induce autoimmune-like antibodies through molecular mimicry, which is famously implicated in rheumatic fever leading to mitral valve regurgitation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Converting plasminogen to plasmin is the action of streptokinase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonspecific cross-linking of T cells and antigen-presenting cells describes the superantigens SPE-A and SPE-C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Degrading connective tissue to facilitate spread describes hyaluronidase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hyaluronic acid capsule is a separate antiphagocytic factor and is not a protein with many immunotypes.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with S. pyogenes cellulitis has infection that is spreading rapidly through the subcutaneous connective tissue of his leg. Which of the following virulence factors most directly facilitates this spread by breaking down connective tissue?

explanation.summary: Hyaluronidase breaks down connective tissue and lets S. pyogenes spread through tissue planes in cellulitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyaluronidase breaks down connective tissue, facilitating spread through tissues and contributing to cellulitis. Streptokinase also aids spread but does so indirectly, by converting plasminogen to plasmin and producing fibrinolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hyaluronic acid capsule gives the organism antiphagocytic properties, not invasive spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M protein blocks complement to inhibit opsonization and phagocytosis rather than digesting tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyrogenic exotoxin A acts as an erythrogenic toxin and superantigen causing scarlet fever and TSLS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptolysin O lyses red and white blood cells and is the target of the ASO titer.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old hospitalized man develops a surgical wound infection. Culture grows a nonhemolytic gram-positive coccus that grows in 6.5% NaCl and is resistant to vancomycin. In addition to wound infections, this organism is most commonly associated with which of the following?

explanation.summary: Enterococci most commonly cause subacute endocarditis and urinary, biliary tract, and wound infections, and VRE is a major nosocomial problem.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium are nonhemolytic and can be grown in 6.5% NaCl media. They most commonly cause subacute endocarditis and urinary, biliary tract, and wound infections. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci are an important cause of nosocomial infection and present a significant treatment challenge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dental caries are caused by viridans streptococci and pharyngitis by S. pyogenes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Necrotizing fasciitis and scarlet fever are caused by S. pyogenes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonatal meningitis and osteomyelitis are characteristic of S. agalactiae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Otitis media and sinusitis are most commonly caused by S. pneumoniae.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is being evaluated for possible acute rheumatic fever, and documentation of a recent group A streptococcal infection is needed. Which of the following serologic tests is the most widely used for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Recent GAS infection is most widely documented with the anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recent infections can be detected with elevated titers of anti-streptolysin O, which is the most widely used test, or with anti-DNase B, anti-hyaluronidase, anti-streptokinase, and anti-M type specific antibodies. Serologic evidence of recent GAS infection is required for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-hyaluronidase titers exist but are not the most widely used assay.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-M type-specific antibodies are listed as an option but are not widely used.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-streptokinase titers are an alternative rather than the standard test.
